html:
In 1872 the Meiji government of Japan issued the Gakusei, an education order that aimed to put every child in school. It said that there should be no family without learning in any village.

The plan borrowed from France for its structure and from the United States for its methods, and was very ambitious: tens of thousands of primary schools across the country. Families had to pay fees and lost children's labour, so some villagers attacked new schools, and the plan was scaled back in the 1880s. Attendance rose steadily all the same, especially once fees were abolished in 1900, and by the early 1900s almost all children went to primary school.

Japan was building on a strong base: in Tokugawa times many commoners had learned to read in small temple schools. Schooling under the empire aimed at loyal subjects as much as skilled workers; the Imperial Rescript on Education of 1890 put loyalty to the emperor at its core. Mass schooling helped Japan industrialise faster than any other non Western country of the time.
